tagline: Pine and hardwood forests frame an interstate over Pine Mountain Ridge.
intro: The I-185 Scenic Byway rolls through mixed pine forest for 38 miles between I-85 and Williams Road, just north of Columbus. Georgia DOT describes gently undulating terrain and opportunities to explore cultural and natural attractions beyond the interstate, including Pine Mountain and Franklin Delano Roosevelt State Park. Georgia DOT’s corridor plan identifies a defining forest relationship: northern Georgia hardwoods meet southern pines here.

Protecting that landscape became a local project in 2005, when government agencies and citizen volunteers began meeting to discuss scenic designation. The Keep Columbus Beautiful Commission coordinated public participation, inviting neighboring property owners and holding community meetings. A larger stakeholder meeting followed in Columbus in January 2006, and community meetings in Pine Mountain and Hamilton brought the proposal to residents and property owners. The application followed in spring 2006 and received approval that summer. Georgia DOT granted byway status in 2007. The designation restricts new billboards along the corridor.

Driving south, begin at I-85 in Troup County’s rolling hills, then follow the interstate through Harris County and over the end of Pine Mountain Ridge. Fields and pastures appear through the evergreens, with occasional views from the road’s high points. The designated drive ends at Exit 12, Williams Road, in northern Muscogee County.

moments.title: Pine Mountain Ridge
moments.text: In Harris County, I-185 climbs over the end of Pine Mountain Ridge. Mixed pine forest borders the road, interrupted by glimpses of agricultural fields and pastures. The corridor’s high points offer occasional views of the surrounding countryside. Georgia DOT’s corridor plan describes a meeting of northern Georgia hardwoods and southern pines along the interstate. Beyond the interstate, GA190 winds along the ridge through F.D. Roosevelt State Park, following a landscape shaped in the 1930s. Roosevelt advocated a scenic highway and park here; as president, he arranged for the Civilian Conservation Corps to build them.

moments.title: Dowdell's Knob
moments.text: A life-size sculpture of Franklin Roosevelt marks the overlook at Dowdell’s Knob in F.D. Roosevelt State Park. Roosevelt first came to this part of Georgia in 1924 to seek relief from polio in the warm springs. He sometimes picnicked on the knob, where he had a brick oven and picnic area built. The bronze sculpture, unveiled in 2007, shows him seated on his removable car seat, wearing leg braces. The knob rises to 1,395 feet, the highest point in the state park. Atlanta sculptor Martin Dawe created it for the Georgia Department of Natural Resources.
moments.notice: Notice Roosevelt’s removable car seat and leg braces in the bronze sculpture.

moments.title: Goat Rock fault
moments.text: North of the Muscogee County line, I-185 crosses the Goat Rock fault. Georgia DOT’s corridor plan identifies a view of the fault here among the route’s geological features.
